One argument for this conclusion contends that the best explanation for systematic disagreement in philosophy is that at least some, potentially all, philosophers are unreliable. Since we do not know who is reliable, we have reason to conclude that we ourselves are probably unreliable. Evidence of one’s potential unreliability in a domain purportedly defeats any first-order support one has for any judgments in that domain. This paper defends philosophy. First, accepting that science is rightfully treated as the benchmark of epistemic progress, I contend that a proper conception of epistemic progress highlights that philosophy and science are relevantly similar in terms of such progress. Secondly, even granting that systematic disagreement is a mark of unreliability and that it does characterize philosophy, this paper further argues that evidence of unreliability is insufficient for meta-level, domain-wide, defeat of philosophical judgments more generally.</jats:p>\", \"DOI\": \"10.5840/eps201956231\", \"type\": \"journal-article\", \"created\": {\"date-parts\": [[2019, 5, 24]], \"date-time\": \"2019-05-24T05:01:27Z\", \"timestamp\": 1558674087000}, \"page\": \"77-94\", \"update-policy\": \"https://doi.org/10.5840/pdc20121120\", \"source\": \"Crossref\", \"is-referenced-by-count\": 2, \"title\": [\"Epistemic Progress Despite Systematic Disagreement\"], \"prefix\": \"10.5840\", \"volume\": \"56\", \"author\": [{\"given\": \"Dustin\", \"family\": \"Olson\", \"sequence\": \"first\", \"affiliation\": [], \"role\": [{\"role\": \"author\", \"vocabulary\": \"crossref\"}]}, {\"name\": \"Institute of Philosophy, Russian Academy of Sciences\", \"seq…
